stance_basis: letter urging bold steps to protect public lands from ORV use and calling for strict regulations
summary: The Idaho Environmental Council, writing from Moscow, Idaho, submitted a letter dated July 22, 1972 opposing unrestricted ORV use on public lands, arguing that the status quo of largely unlimited off-road vehicle access must change. They enclosed a presentation by one of their directors detailing environmental harms from ORVs and calling for specific regulatory steps including trail closures, noise limits, and snowmobile restrictions in wildlife wintering areas. The Council urged federal land administrators to take bold protective action before problems worsen, and argued that public lands are not playgrounds for machines.
complaint_summary: An enclosed presentation by Idaho Environmental Council director Carl J. Hocevar details environmental harms from ORV use including soil erosion, wildlife harassment, and noise pollution, and proposes specific regulatory steps such as immediate trail closures, snowmobile restrictions in wildlife wintering areas, and noise level limits of 70-75 db.

statement.text:
Idaho Environmental Council
P. O. Box 3371 - University Station Moscove, Idaha 83843
February 18, 1971
Presented to Panel -- "Off-Hoad Vehicle Use of Public Lands"
Upper Snake River Chapter of the Federal Executive Association
by Carl J. Hocevar
The increasing use of off-road vehicles is presenting problems that must be recognized and dealt with by land management agencies. The time to consider and solve the problems is before they become uncontrollable.
Before one can attack a problem he must identify it. In the first part of my presentation I will present the problem areas associated with the use of off-road vehicles as seen by conservationists. Having identified the problems I will then describe some efforts designed to regulate the use of off-road vehicles in other parts of the country. Finally, I will propose steps that should be taken locally to regulate off-road vehicle use.
I. What are the problems?
In general the problems created by the use of off-road vehicles may be classified in three categories: (1) damage to soil and vegetation. (2) impact on wildlife, and (3) esthetic considerations.
Trailbikes and four wheel drive vehicles are the cause of soil erosion in many areas. This is especially true where the vehicles are used indiscriminantly in granitic soils and in high alpine areas. Wet meadou areas are quite susceptible to damage by motorized vehicles. Long deep ruts are cut into these areas resulting in erosion paths. Even if used on trails these vehicles may cause severe erosion, especially if the trails are on steep slopes.
At this time I would like to show a few slides depicting soil damage caused by trailbikes in the Caribou National Forest.

Soil erosion problems may be compounded by the introduction of several new vehicles. A two-wheel drive trailcycle is now on the market. Even more frightening is the all terrain vehicle. These vehicles may be appropriately referred to as miniature tanks and they will do just about as much damage to the terrain as their big brothers.
Large areas of land are no longer safe from damage after the snow falls; the propositing season is then just beginning. In some areas enoughbles are used on thin layers of snow. Grasses and undergrowth may be torn up in these areas and small shrubs may be exushed if the snow is not deep enough to cover them. In many instances the damage is done inadvertently and the snowhobilers may not even be aware of the damage they are doing.
The impact of off-road vehicles on wildlife is becoming more of a problem, especially with the advent of the snow-mobile. Besides using snowmobiles to get into the backcountry some indiscrete hunters also use them to chase animals and may actually run deer to exhaustion.
Wildlife harassment does not end with the close of the hunting season since, unfortunately, some of the most accessible snowmobiling areas are also some of the best big game wintering areas. During the midwinter and early spring months the anommobiling activities are at their peak. This period also coincides with the time when the animals are also the least mobile and the most vulnerable from a physical standpoint. The wildlife in their winter ranges have a tough time just surviving without having to contend with harassment from snowmobilers. It does not take much exertion to cause animals to contract pneumonia once they are in their weakened condition. Any form of harassment is particularly hard on pregnant females.
Not all harassment of wildlife is done maliciously, but much is done by thoughtless individuals who are only trying to get close enough to photograph or observe the anitals. Neverthôless, the game is still frightened by the noise and the mobility of the snowpobiles. Shew whilers any inadvertently scare wildlife just by being in the same vicinity. The transmendous racket made by these machines carries long distances and disturbs the anitals.
I do not know whether there has been a problem in Ideho of people chasing courans or predators such as coyates, but this practice has been a problem in other parts of the country. This type of problem could easily occur if it does not already exist.
Smaller forms of wildlife may also be adversely affected by snowmebiles. A noted Canadian wildlife expert. Philip Corbet, has noted that show is an excellent insulator and a natural protection for sice and other small animals. When the snow is packed down by snowmobiles it loses its insulating qualities thereby reducing protection for the such each animals.

The use of off-road vehicles increases hunting pressures in many areas which were formerly inaccessible to most hunters. These refuges are lost then retorized vehicles are used to bring in larger numbers of heaters.
Index is being compromised by the use of motorized vehicles. The principal value of these lands lies in their ability to provide primitive type experience for an increasing number of people. Here people are beginning to look to our public lands as a means of escape from the procesures of medern living. They are looking for colitude or at least a minimum of disturbance. However, even in the backcountry silence is becoming much more difficult to find as recreational motorized vehicles are increasing in numbers. People are continually being affronted by noisy trailbikes and snow obiles. Even a small number of these vehicles can reduce the enjoyment others may derive from the use of our public lands.
Is noise a real problem? Very definitely. It is recognized as one of our major forms of pollution. Loud noises are not only annoying and disturbing but can also cause damage to hearing. To give us an idea of what noise levels we are talking about I will first list some thresholds and then list the noise levels generated by a number of familiar situations. one additional potential problem areas I would like to mention one additional potential problem area that I can foresce. This is not an immediate problem but is included to provide an example of things to come. I am referring to the one-men flying platform. This vehicle is jet powered and is capable of transporting people at up to 60 mph. This vehicle will be a real noise polluter and could possibly be used to but form. I think we may be seeing these vehicles on the market within the next ten years.

II. What is being done around the country to regulate the use of off-road vehicles?
We have heard this morning from the Park Service and the Forest Service concerning the edministration of off-road vehicles in Yelloustone Park and in the Tarthee National Porest. I would now like to present additional information concerning attempts to regulate the use of off-road vehicles in other parts of the country.
The control of snowmebiles is attracting attention throughout the snowbelt regions of the United States. There are over 1000 miles of snowmobile trails in the national forests in the eastern part of the United States. By designating appropriate trails the Forest Service is controlling the areas in which snowmobilers go thus avoiding conflicts with wildlife.
Several of the national forests in Washington have closed trails to snowmobiles.
In January, 1971, an area around Sun Valley was closed to snowmobile use due to damage done to ski areas, vegetation, and watersheds.
Some state and local governments are using registration fees to lay out trails in parks and in state forests. As of January, 1969 Michigan had built 500 miles of trails and had plans for an additional 1300 miles by 1973.
The state of New York currently has legislation pending that would limit muffler noise from snowmobiles to 73 db.
On February 8. 1971 President Nixon presented a package of environmental bills to Congress. Included was a noise pollution regulation pertaining to snowmobiles.
Although trailbikes are a problem in all the western states the coastal states have taken the load in trailbike regulation. In California 6 of the 18 national forests have off-road vehicle restrictions. In late 1969 sinteen percent of the trails in non-wilderness areas had been closed to vehicles. The principal reason given was soil erosion but conflicts with non-vehicle users also was a factor.
Colorado has closed about 85 of the trails in non-wilderness areas to four-wheel drive vehicles due to resource damage and to conflicts with foot and horse travellers and compers.
In June, 1970, the Menatchee National Forest in Washington had closed 89 trails to all motorized vehicles. Ten trails were closed to four-wheel drive vehicles. In addition, certain areas were also closed to cross-country use of vehicles.

In March, 1969, the Snequalmic National Forest, also in Washington, had closed 11 trails and has considering the closure of 25 additional trails.
In Oregon, the Deschutes National Forest closed 42 trails and in addition closed the entire Broken Top area to trailbikes. These restrictions want into effect on April 15, 1970.
In Idaho the only closure to trailbikes in a non-wilderness area that I know of is in the Mallard-Larkins Pieneer Area in the St. Joe National Porest.
In the western slopes of the Tetons the trail to Alaska Basin has also been closed to trailbikes.
III. What should be done to regulate the use of off-road vehicles. 
1. Trails should be closed to trailbikes immediately where soil erosion is currently a problem.
2. Trails should be closed to trailbites immediately where there are conflicts with non-vehicle users.
3. Where it appears that persistent use of trailbikes will damage fragile soils then trails should be closed.
4. Trail closures should be effected if potential conflicts with increasing numbers of hikers and horses seems inevitable.
5. In general, off-trail use of trailbikes should be eliminated. It is particularly important that trail cycles not be allowed on high alpine meadous. Certain areas may be designated for cross country use if soil damage is not deemed to be a problem and if conflicts with other groups will not be a problem.
6. Four-wheel drive vehicles should be restricted to well established roads or four-wheel drive trails where there is no drager of soil erosion.
7. Snowmobiles should not be allowed in areas that are prime wintering grounds for wildlife.
8. Trails should be established for snowmobile use. This practice will insure that snowmobiles are not used in wintering areas and will minimize conflicts with other groups.
9. Certain high country areas should be established where snowmobiles are not allowed. In these areas other groups such as ski tourers may enjoy quiet surroundings. Zoning 73 areas for snowmobile use will insure that more than one recreational user group will be satisfied.
